analysis.one_liner: Blocks federal funding for consumer, environmental, health, labor, and financial rules, and puts the consumer bureau on the annual budget.
analysis.headline: Introduced January 12, 2016 with 25 Republican cosponsors, the bill was sent to 13 House committees, never received a hearing, markup, or vote, and died when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would reopen the 2016 government funding law and bolt on dozens of riders, each one barring federal agencies from spending money on a specific rule. It would cut off the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's independent funding and make it ask Congress for money, block the Labor Department rule requiring financial advisers to put retirement savers' interests first, stop the EPA's climate, water, ozone, and fracking rules, freeze workplace safety and union election rules, protect for-profit colleges from the gainful-employment rule, and bar regulators from limiting broadband prices or data caps. It also includes an immigration title cutting federal grants to sanctuary cities and a land exchange for a road in an Alaska wildlife refuge.
analysis.who_benefits: Banks and large financial firms (the consumer bureau would depend on annual appropriations, and the Senate's Financial Regulatory Improvement Act would be enacted wholesale), oil, gas, and coal companies (climate, water, ozone, and fracking rules unfunded), financial advisers and annuity sellers (the fiduciary rule unfunded), broadband providers (no price or data-cap regulation), for-profit colleges (gainful-employment rule unfunded), tobacco and e-cigarette makers (the 2007 grandfather date reset to the later deeming-regulation date), and operators of long double-trailer truck combinations (length limit raised from 28 to 33 feet).
analysis.who_benefits_short: Banks, fossil fuel producers, financial advisers, broadband and tobacco firms

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's independent funding stream and instead requires annual appropriations, quarterly reports to Congress, and advance notice of fund transfers [S3].
Enacts Title IX of S. 1910, the Financial Regulatory Improvement Act of 2015, into law, a broad package of financial regulatory changes [S3].
Bars funding to finalize or enforce the Labor Department's fiduciary rule requiring retirement investment advisers to act in clients' best interest [S3].

Bars funding to propose, finalize, implement, or enforce EPA greenhouse gas standards for power plants, the Waters of the United States definition, the federal hydraulic fracturing rule, stricter ozone standards, and use of the social cost of carbon [S3].
Bars funding to implement the education department's gainful employment rule aimed at poor-performing for-profit college programs [S3].
Bars funding to regulate the prices, fees, or data caps charged by broadband internet providers, reversing the FCC's 2015 open internet order approach on those points [S3].
Changes the tobacco deeming rule so that e-cigarettes and other newly regulated products keep the pre-2007 grandfather treatment rather than facing premarket review [S3].
Amends truck size limits to allow 33-foot (rather than 28-foot) trailers in double-trailer combinations, and blocks the DOT's airline ancillary fee transparency rulemaking [S3].
Bars DHS grants to sanctuary jurisdictions and makes jurisdictions that limit immigration-status cooperation ineligible for DOJ COPS and Byrne-JAG grants; also halts expansion of DACA and DAPA [S3].

Authorizes a land exchange with Alaska to build a single-lane gravel road through the Izembek National Wildlife Refuge between King Cove and Cold Bay for emergency medical access, and declares it not a major federal action under NEPA [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Retirement savers would keep paying conflicted advice fees; consumers and small investors would lose the consumer bureau's independent watchdog funding; workers exposed to respirable crystalline silica would wait for an OSHA limit while a new National Academy of Sciences study is commissioned; low-income households would lose Housing Trust Fund transfers and the Affirmatively Furthering Fair Housing rule; broadband customers would lose price and data-cap protections; families in sanctuary jurisdictions could lose local public safety grants; and the public would bear the health and environmental costs of unfunded clean air, water, climate, and fracking rules.
analysis.who_pays_short: Retirement savers, consumers, workers, and communities

drawbacks.text: Section 303 would bar any agency from publishing or disseminating any regulation, guidance, or order that imposes a legal obligation, which on its face would prevent agencies from issuing binding rules at all, far beyond the individual rules targeted elsewhere in the bill [S3].

Ending the consumer bureau's independent funding would make its budget hostage to annual appropriations and quarterly reporting, weakening the agency created after the 2008 financial crisis to police consumer financial products [S3].

Blocking the fiduciary rule, the silica rule, the gainful employment rule, and net neutrality price regulation each imposes a direct cost on retirement savers, silica-exposed workers, student borrowers, and broadband customers [S3].

Proponents would acknowledge that the sanctuary-cities grant cutoffs and the ban on third parties joining OSHA inspections carry real trade-offs in local law enforcement funding and workplace oversight [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits flow almost entirely to regulated industries, in the form of rules that never take effect and agencies that cannot enforce them. The costs are diffuse but real: weaker retirement-advice standards, delayed workplace safety limits, reduced consumer and internet-price protections, and unfunded environmental rules. The provision barring agencies from publishing any binding regulation at all goes beyond targeted relief and would grind ordinary rulemaking to a halt.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to 13 House committees and several subcommittees, none of which ever scheduled action, and it expired when the 114th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ken Buck (R-CO) introduced the bill on January 12, 2016 [S5].

It was referred that day to the Financial Services Committee and twelve other committees: Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Foreign Affairs, Oversight and Government Reform, Natural Resources, the Judiciary, Homeland Security, Transportation and Infrastructure, Education and the Workforce, Agriculture, Budget, and Rules [S5].

In the following days it was referred to subcommittees on Aviation, Economic Development and Public Buildings, Highways and Transit, Water Resources, Health, Energy and Mineral Resources, Federal Lands, and Water, Power and Oceans [S5].
The record shows no hearing, markup, committee vote, floor action, or roll call before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers, retirement savers, and the public-health and environmental rules the bill targeted stayed in place; the industries that would have gained from the riders got nothing. The bill's supporters left with a statement of priorities but no law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumers and savers; the riders died in committee

for.name: 25 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 25 listed cosponsors were Republicans

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on January 12, 2016; the record shows no markup, hearing, or vote on the bill before Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: All 25 cosponsors were Republicans and the sponsor was a Republican; no Democrat signed on, and the bill never reached the floor for a recorded vote.

industries.note: The bill would end the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's independent funding, make it seek appropriations with quarterly reporting, make it harder for the Financial Stability Oversight Council to designate nonbank firms for supervision, and enact the Financial Regulatory Improvement Act. Ordinary consumers lose an independently funded watchdog and firms gain a lighter oversight regime.

The bill would defund the Clean Power Plan and other power-plant greenhouse gas standards, the Waters of the United States definition, the fracking rule on federal lands, stricter ozone standards, and the social cost of carbon, and bar trade agreements limiting U.S. emissions. The public bears the resulting air, water, and climate costs.

industries.industry: Financial advisers and annuity and insurance sellers
industries.note: Blocking the Labor Department's fiduciary rule lets advisers continue selling higher-commission retirement products without a best-interest standard; savers bear the difference in fees and returns.

The bill resets the grandfather date so newly deemed tobacco products, including e-cigarettes, avoid premarket review for products on the market at the later deeming date, keeping them on shelves without FDA authorization review.
The gainful employment rule, which cut federal aid to programs whose graduates could not repay loans, would be unfunded, leaving student borrowers in weak programs without that protection.
The bill bars any funding to regulate the prices, fees, or data caps of broadband service, removing the main consumer-protection lever over internet pricing under the 2015 open internet framework.

industries.industry: Trucking operators of long double-trailer combinations
industries.note: Raising the allowable trailer length from 28 to 33 feet in double-trailer combinations benefits carriers using longer rigs; safety reviewers have long questioned bigger trucks on shared roads.

The bill would freeze the NLRB's streamlined representation-election rule, keep the pre-2014 joint-employer standard, bar third-party representatives from joining OSHA walkaround inspections, and delay the silica exposure limit pending a new study. Workers lose the protections at the same time unions do.

industries.industry: Affordable housing programs and fair housing enforcement
industries.note: The bill would bar any funds from being transferred or credited to the Housing Trust Fund and block the Affirmatively Furthering Fair Housing rule, cutting off resources for low-income housing and local fair-housing planning.

industries.industry: State and local governments with sanctuary policies
industries.note: The bill would make such jurisdictions ineligible for FEMA state and local grants, COPS, and Byrne-JAG funding and for SCAAP contracts. Supporters frame this as immigration enforcement; the cost falls on those jurisdictions' residents and budgets.
